title: Trajectory warmup & evacuation playbook — PRD sketch
body:
Context and intent:
This doc sketches a complementary approach to existing dedicated-capacity autoscaling work: instead of reacting purely to instantaneous load or simple rate-based headroom, use short-horizon demand trajectories to proactively warm compute and KV-cache state, and coordinate graceful evacuation when capacity must be reclaimed. Purpose is operational predictability + fewer cold-token penalties during bursts, while preserving tenant isolation guarantees.

Problem statement (why this is needed):
- Ramp-ups cause token-level latency spikes: cold KV caches + kernel scheduling penalties.
- Traditional warm pools (static or predictive) are either too coarse (wastes capacity) or too slow (misses bursts).
- During forced preemption (eviction, spot reclaim) naive eviction causes large-scale latency/regression for affected tenants.
- Existing approaches handle autoscale and warm pools, but not an integrated trajectory-driven warmup + structured evacuation protocol that respects isolation tags and SLA windows.

Key idea (summary):
- Use a short-horizon trajectory model (1–20 minute horizon) per-tenant/workload fingerprint to predict likelihood and magnitude of near-term demand.
- Translate trajectory into two coordinated actions: (1) staged warmup (pre-spawn workers, prefill KV prefixes, attach warmed quantized weights) and (2) graded evacuation (if capacity needs reclaiming, evacuate low-priority lanes first with state handoff and graceful throttle windows).
- The orchestrator exposes knobs and safety checks for tenancy isolation: warmup budget per tenant, max borrowable headroom, and evacuation grace windows by SLO tier.

Behavioral goals / non-goals:
- Goals: reduce 95/99 token latency spikes on ramp-ups by >30% for workloads with predictable regularity; limit wasted reserved compute to <10% in steady state; ensure evacuation events do not breach critical-tier SLOs.
- Non-goals: do not replace long-term predictive capacity planning or billing model changes. This is an operational runtime policy layer.

Trajectory model (brief):
- Inputs: recent per-tenant request rate time-series (5s granularity), session-concurrency, model variant, spot/priority tier, calendar signals (CRON-like schedules), active campaigns flagged by CS.
- Output: probability distribution over delta-QPS over 1/5/15 minute horizons plus a confidence band.
- Implementation options: lightweight ensemble (EWMA + FFT anomaly detector + tiny LSTM) or simple gradient-boosted regression using moving-window features. Preference: start with interpretable hybrid (EWMA + feature rules) to keep operator control.

Warmup primitives (what the platform will do):
- warm_rate: fraction of a worker fleet to pre-allocate per predicted delta-QPS (configurable per-tenant, default 0.1).
- kv_prefill: specify prefixes (or example prompts) used to prime KV cache; run in low-cost prefill mode (no billing to tenant while prefill is in standby).
- staged_attach: sequence to attach quantized model shards and load weights with staggered gc windows to reduce IO contention.
- cooldown_ttl: how long a warmed worker remains warm without traffic before being eligible for decommit.
- borrowable_headroom: max headroom a tenant may borrow from shared warm pool; tracked in a ledger to prevent abuse.

Evacuation modes (tiered):
1) gentle-drain (preferred): redirect new requests to fallback model variant and stream in-progress KV to sticky cache; keep existing workers serving until idle; used for burst smoothing where immediate capacity reclaim is not essential.
2) staged-evac: proactively migrate hot prefixes to other workers and progressively drop low-priority queues over grace windows (30s -> 2m -> 5m).
3) hard-preempt: immediate stop + fast fallback invocation; only for critical infra events (e.g., host failure, emergency decommit).

Isolation rules and safety constraints:
- isolation_tags: per-tenant metadata (critical, gold, silver, bronze) used to compute evacuation priority.
- per-tenant headroom caps: a fixed soft cap, then throttling rules once exceeded.
- cross-tenant prefill limits: limit concurrent KV prefill tasks to prevent shared IO saturation.
- rollback condition: if warmup causes downstream degradation (increased queueing, IO saturation), abort warmup and revert workers to decomm.

APIs / config surface (developer-facing):
- autoscale.trajectory_horizon: 1m|5m|15m (default 5m)
- autoscale.warm_rate: float [0,1]
- autoscale.kv_prefill_list: list of example prompts/keys
- autoscale.borrowable_headroom: tokens or compute-seconds
- autoscale.evacuation_mode: gentle|staged|hard
- admin.run_playbook(reason, tenant, mode) — operator trigger for manual warmup/evacuation

Operator runbook (day-to-day and incident):
- Normal ops: monitor Trajectory Dashboard (per-tenant predicted delta + warmup budget). Alerts: predicted delta > X and warm_rate==0 => ops/SE runbook to check billing/contract.
- Incident: host OOM spike during warmup -> immediate abort warmup and reduce concurrent prefill cap.
- Evacuation event: if staged-evac triggered unexpectedly, run triage: (1) check isolation_tag assignment, (2) inspect headroom ledger, (3) audit recent config commits.
- Postmortem checklist: timeline of trajectory signal -> warmup actions -> observed metrics (latency, queueing, failed warmups), root cause, proposed fix.

Evaluation plan / success metrics:
- Baseline: measure 95/99 token latency and tail percentiles during known ramp windows for a set of tenants.
- Launch pilot: choose 6 tenants across tiers (2 critical, 2 gold, 2 bronze) with normal weekly bursts.
- Success criteria after 4 weeks: median warmup overhead < 8% extra reserved compute; 95th token latency improvement >= 25% for planned bursts; no critical-tier SLA breaches due to eviction.
- Telemetry to collect: prefill IO ops, warm attach durations, per-tenant headroom ledger ops, warm_failure_rate, evacuation_fallthrough_count.

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- Billing & billing signals: do we charge for prefill compute? (pro: cost recovery; con: developer friction). Consider free warm budget for first N minutes per month.
- Model of confidence: how aggressive should warm_rate be at low confidence? Conservative by default, with opt-in aggressive mode for enterprise partners.
- Data privacy: KV prefill uses example prompts — ensure no customer PII is inadvertently used in shared prefill processes.
- Implementation complexity: how much of this lives in the control plane vs. the dedicated runtime? Prefer split: lightweight decision in control plane, heavy lifting inside runtime agents.

Rough rollout plan:
1) Prototype trajectory detector + warm_rate simulator (2 weeks).
2) Small-scale pilot with 3 tenants (1 week prep + 3 weeks pilot). Monitor metrics.
3) Expand to wider cohort; add evacuation staged mode and operator tooling (6 weeks).
4) Post-launch: iterate on confidence heuristics and billing policy (ongoing).

Notes / loose ideas (brainstorm fragments):
- Could integrate customer-provided signals (webhooks when marketing campaigns start).
- Consider warm-rate auctions for spare pool when multiple tenants request overlapping warmups. Ledger-based settlement to keep fairness.
- Maybe expose a "boost token" to customers for one-off aggressive warmups.

References / links:
- Related tickets: INFRA-2376 (trajectory infra), DEDICATED-934 (evacuation api stub)
- Prototype PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/inference-orchestration/pull/482
- Slack thread: #dedicated-autoscale (see pinned messages Feb 2025)

Next steps (for this draft):
- Align with runtime team on feasibility of staged_attach and kv_prefill IO budgets (action: @Liam O'Connell).
- Wire up basic trajectory detector in telemetry sandbox and run backtests on historical tenant traffic (action: @Diego Morales).
- Schedule product/solutions sync with two pilot customers to capture opt-in signals and acceptable billing semantics (@Priya Nair).

Questions for reviewers:
- Are the proposed evacuation windows (30s/2m/5m) reasonable or too long for interactive SLAs?
- Is a shared warm pool with ledgered debt acceptable from a security/isolation standpoint?
- Any obvious throughput/IO saturation scenarios we missed?

(End of sketch — keep messy notes here; will formalize into a PRD if pilot metrics look promising.)
